frameworks.name: 12 Internal Copy Hacks
frameworks.definition: Alex Hormozi's internal checklist of 12 (plus one bonus) principles applied to every piece of advertising copy, covering headlines, specificity, proof, trust, urgency, authority, CTAs, and readability.

frameworks.name: How to Yay Without Boo Headline Template
frameworks.definition: A headline formula structured as: 'How to [desired outcome] without [feared obstacle], even if [biggest insecurity].' Combines benefit, objection preemption, and empathy in one clause.

frameworks.name: What-Who-When Status Framework
frameworks.definition: A copy-writing framework (documented in Hormozi's Leads book, p.140) that dimensions status by: What the benefit is, Who awards the status (family, rivals, colleagues), and When (past, present, future).

frameworks.name: Five-Stage Awareness Stack
frameworks.definition: Eugene Schwartz's customer awareness ladder applied to ad targeting: Unaware (hook with curiosity) -> Problem Aware (name the symptom) -> Solution Aware (prior failed attempts) -> Product Aware (category comparison) -> Most Aware (direct offer). Each level requires a different hook.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the headline is the single highest-leverage element in any advertisement: moving from a 1% to a 3% click-through rate via a better headline triples the audience who sees all subsequent content, and a winning headline can outperform a control by 2-5x — a lift impossible to achieve through any other single funnel variable.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: any paid or organic advertising format with a visible headline or hook
claims.mechanism: The headline is a law-of-small-numbers lever: a multiplier on click-through rate propagates through every downstream conversion step, so even a 3x CTR lift from a headline improvement has more absolute impact than a 50% lift at any later funnel stage.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that competitors can copy an offer but they cannot copy proof — proof (documented results, real testimonials, verifiable stories) must be earned, not replicated — and in an AI-saturated environment where trust is eroding, verified real-world experience becomes the primary differentiator because AI avatars can lie but cannot have actually done something.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: markets with rising AI-generated content
any category where trust verification is possible
claims.mechanism: Proof is non-replicable because it requires prior real-world action; as trust in content erodes due to AI proliferation, verification of real-world results becomes scarcer and therefore more valuable, widening the gap between proof-holders and promise-makers.
bounded_by: Does not apply where proof is legally restricted (NDA, compliance)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that explicitly calling out who an offer is NOT for is more powerful than calling out who it is for, because it communicates strong marketplace positioning, polarizes the right customer toward the offer, and eliminates the vanilla problem — being everything to all people means no one feels the offer is specifically for them.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: calling out who you're not looking for
conditions: any direct-response or paid advertising context
markets with sufficient volume that excluding a segment still leaves an addressable pool
claims.mechanism: Specificity of exclusion signals confidence and positioning depth; prospects who remain after the exclusion self-select as high-fit leads, reducing wasted impressions and increasing conversion among those who continue.
bounded_by: Requires sufficient total market volume so the excluded segment does not deplete the addressable base below viability

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that damaging admissions — openly stating a product's flaws before making claims — are the single most powerful persuasion technique available in copywriting, because admitting bias upfront increases believability of all subsequent claims and the linguistic structure 'X [flaw], but Y [benefit]' transfers credibility from the acknowledged truth to the benefit that follows the word 'but'.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: any advertising or sales copy context
products or services with knowable, observable flaws
claims.mechanism: Acknowledging a flaw pre-empts the prospect's internal objection, and the act of honesty about the flaw signals reliability; the sentence structure 'A but B' causes the reader to weight B more heavily, so placing the benefit after 'but' compounds the trust transfer into persuasion.
bounded_by: The flaw admitted must be real and not catastrophic to the core value proposition — admitting a fatal flaw does not flip to credibility

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that the word 'because' is one of the most influential words in the English language for advertising: research (attributed to Cialdini) shows that providing any reason — even a non-sequitur — significantly increases compliance compared to providing no reason at all.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: any request for compliance embedded in copy or sales conversations
claims.mechanism: Humans have a cognitive pattern of treating reason-giving as legitimate justification; the presence of a causal connector ('because') activates compliance heuristics even when the specific reason provided has no logical force.
bounded_by: Bonus points when the reason connects to genuine urgency or scarcity rather than a contrived one

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that specificity — describing the precise physical or emotional moment a person experiences a problem — is more persuasive than category-level language, because the reader experiences the moment as addressed to them personally, lowering the action threshold.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: any audience-facing copy in B2C or B2B contexts
when the writer has direct experience with the audience's problem
claims.mechanism: General language ('are you overweight?') is recognized as marketing-speak and triggers skeptical processing; moment-specific language ('do you sweat in places you didn't know you could when you walk upstairs?') bypasses that filter because it reads as intimate knowledge, creating a 'he knows my secret' response that lowers buyer resistance.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that benefit-to-status framing — tying product benefits to the social standing they produce within a specific peer group — is a more persuasive framing than stating benefits alone, because humans are wired to seek status as a resource-acquisition signal within their subgroup.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: any consumer or business product advertising
when the benefit can plausibly confer visible social proof in the buyer's peer group
claims.mechanism: Status desire is an evolutionary driver (resource acquisition and reproduction); tying product benefits to visible status outcomes within the buyer's specific reference group (family, colleagues, rivals) converts abstract benefits into emotionally activating social proof.
bounded_by: Status reference group must match the specific avatar — e.g., Lamborghini status is relevant to 20-year-old hustle-bro avatars, not to mothers

claims.text: Alex Hormozi distinguishes scarcity (a function of limited quantity) from urgency (a function of limited time), and asserts that either only works — and maintains power across repeated campaigns — if it is legitimate: enforcing the limit when it is reached is the only mechanism that preserves future credibility and converts the person who missed the first offer into the first buyer of the next.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: any promotional offer in B2C or B2B advertising
claims.mechanism: False urgency or scarcity that is not enforced trains the audience that limits are fictitious, permanently depressing future conversion; real enforcement of the limit creates a pool of disappointed buyers who self-select as highest-intent prospects for the next campaign.
bounded_by: Requires the seller to actually say no to post-deadline buyers, which most sellers avoid

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for any written sales copy, the headline and the PS statement are the two most-read sections, making them together the highest-leverage pair of copy elements, and that the PPS statement is the third most-read section.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: long-form email copy
direct-response landing pages and sales letters

numbers.axis: read-rate rank within a piece of long-form copy

bounded_by: Specific to long-form text copy; less applicable to short-form social ad formats

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that say-do correspondence — telling the prospect exactly what will happen next and then delivering that outcome — compounds influence over time, because each fulfilled prediction causes the prospect to be more likely to follow future instructions, analogous to how Martha Stewart built outsized influence by giving precise recipes that reliably produced promised results.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: multi-step funnels where the prospect must take sequential actions
any advertiser with repeated audience exposure (email list, retargeting)
claims.mechanism: Each prediction-fulfillment cycle activates classical conditioning: prospect follows instruction, desired outcome occurs, trust in the instructor increases, next instruction triggers faster compliance. The effect compounds across cycles and is the mechanism behind why CTAs that describe the next step lift conversion.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that keeping copy at a third-grade reading level — rather than a ninth-grade level — maximizes the reading audience and thus conversion, because pausing to decode a difficult word or sentence causes readers to stop reading, and most people who can read cannot process ninth-grade text at ad-scrolling speed.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: paid advertising copy in any format
email, video sales letters, landing pages, cold outreach
claims.mechanism: Reading-level friction raises cognitive cost at a moment when the reader is already distracted and moving fast; the moment comprehension requires active processing, behavioral momentum breaks and the prospect disengages before the CTA.

numbers.axis: reading level and estimated audience reachability

anchors.value: excludes roughly two-thirds of potential readers

bounded_by: Simplicity takes priority over concision when they conflict — a shorter but harder word is worse than a longer but common word

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that combining entertainment and education in advertising produces better outcomes than either alone: entertainment expands reach by making content broadly shareable, while education changes behavior (the click, the purchase), and the two together are the formula for ads that are both seen widely and acted upon.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: paid and organic advertising contexts
when the advertiser can actually be funny or entertaining, as humor cannot be forced
claims.mechanism: Entertainment lowers psychological resistance to persuasion by generating positive affect; education delivers the belief-change required to motivate a specific action; humor is the highest-leverage vehicle for entertainment but also the hardest to engineer and the first element to cut if resources are constrained.
bounded_by: Humor is optional and should be cut before the other 12 elements if production constraints exist
Effective humor requires extensive testing across audience segments, as comedians do across venues

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that implied authority — longevity signals, volume claims, minor awards, and pro-athlete name-drops — is effective in advertising because people trust and comply with authority figures more readily, and even a minor local award creates a conversational credibility hook that changes how prospects receive the pitch.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: any direct-response advertising or sales conversation
service businesses where personal trust is a purchase barrier
claims.mechanism: Authority signals (longevity, volume, third-party recognition) activate a compliance heuristic: people defer judgment to perceived experts. Even low-prestige signals ('Best Boot Camp in Vegas', a minor local list) are sufficient to shift the frame in a sales conversation from stranger to endorsed expert.
bounded_by: Prospect must first want the outcome being offered before authority signals become persuasive — authority matters at the believability stage, not the desire stage

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that advertising to the masses via generic language ('are you overweight?') fails because no individual feels specifically addressed, whereas writing copy directed at a single specific person — naming their exact sensory moments and private experiences — creates a 'how does he know my secrets?' reaction that is the hallmark of compelling, converting copy.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: any direct-response copy targeting a definable avatar
claims.mechanism: Generic language triggers pattern-matching to 'ad' and is filtered out; moment-specific language that names private sensory details (sweating in unexpected places, a bar that looks like a bomb went off) reads as insider knowledge, bypassing the ad-recognition filter and creating felt personal relevance.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a 4.6-star rating with 4,000 reviews outperforms a 5-star rating with 3 reviews in a consumer purchasing decision, because the volume of reviews is the real authority signal — it implies longevity, scale, and operational reliability — whereas a perfect rating on a small sample reads as unverified.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: consumer selection contexts where review volume is visible (Yelp, Google, Amazon)
claims.mechanism: High review volume implies that the business has served many customers over time, which is itself an authority and trust signal; a perfect score on a tiny sample does not carry the same implied longevity.

numbers.axis: review volume vs. rating score as trust driver

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that in comedy (and by analogy, in advertising), material quality is validated through iterative testing across multiple audience segments — comedians develop a 60-minute set by continuously culling to the best-performing minutes across many venues — rather than through a priori judgment, and the same testing discipline should apply to identifying winning copy angles and humor in ads.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: advertising creative development
humor writing for ads
claims.mechanism: No single writer can pre-judge which joke or copy angle will land universally; only live audience response across varied segments reveals true performance; iteration toward the surviving material is the only path to a reliably high-converting set.

numbers.axis: material culling in comedy set development

anchors.value: ~8 minutes of material that audiences liked
entire 60 minutes refined to reliably land

examples.text: Hormozi illustrates the headline CTR multiplier with a concrete funnel math example: if a headline change moves click-through rate from 1% to 3%, it triples the number of people who see all downstream content. He contrasts this with typical A/B test wins of 20-50% at later funnel stages, noting that a 3x improvement is nearly impossible to achieve anywhere else in the funnel except at the headline level.

To illustrate damaging admissions and the 'but' sentence structure, Hormozi offers three compressed examples: (1) 'These markers smell like shit, but they write four times longer than other markers and don't dry out' — the flaw admission makes the durability claim more believable. (2) The reverse, 'These markers write four times longer, but they smell like crap,' emphasizes the flaw, not the benefit. (3) 'Our websites are ugly as hell, but they convert' versus 'Our websites convert, but they're ugly' — demonstrating how the clause after 'but' receives the credibility transfer from the clause before it.

Hormozi offers a gym example to illustrate damaging admissions applied to local advertising: 'Our gym has honestly pretty terrible parking. Our AC is kind of on and off. I don't have the best equipment, but our sessions are more fun than everyone else's because it's all we've got.' He argues a viewer would respond: 'I kind of believe this guy. He's probably not so bad.' In contrast, the claim 'We have the most fun sessions' triggers immediate skepticism because anyone can make it.

Hormozi gives a Cialdini-sourced example to illustrate why reasons matter independent of their quality. In a line-cutting study, people allowed others to cut in line when given a reason tied to urgency ('I need to copy something quickly, I have a paper due'). But a subsequent test showed that a nonsense reason ('because my cat is back home') also increased compliance significantly versus no reason at all. The word 'because' plus any completing clause activated the compliance heuristic.

To illustrate moment-specific copy in the weight loss category, Hormozi contrasts 'Are you overweight?' (category-level, marketing-speak) with 'Do you have trouble getting upstairs or going on a walk for a long period of time without a rash forming between your legs and sweating in places you didn't know you could?' — the latter describes a specific lived moment that a qualifying reader has almost certainly experienced recently, making the pain feel fresh and lowering the action threshold.

Hormozi describes a bar consulting client whose copy used generic marketing language. He reframes it using moment-specificity: instead of describing bar efficiency generically, the copy should ask 'When you look behind the bar, does it look like a bomb went off? Does it look like a homeless shelter back there?' He reasons that bar owners who have this problem have almost certainly experienced that moment in the last seven days, making the pain fresh and increasing likelihood of action.

To illustrate status-benefit framing, Hormozi gives the cookbook example: rather than saying 'you'll cook meals fast and easy,' the status-framed version is 'a cookbook so fast and easy that all your friends will wonder how you found the time to be fit and cook for your family.' The benefit (fast cooking) is unchanged, but the status award (friends' admiration) adds a social desirability layer that converts the rational benefit into an emotionally activating outcome.

Hormozi uses Martha Stewart as the canonical example of say-do correspondence compounding influence: Stewart gave precise recipes (explicit instructions), promised outcomes ('follow these 18 steps and you get a cake'), the outcomes materialized (the cake tasted good), and then social reinforcement followed ('your family loves you for baking this cake'). Each cycle of instruction-followed-by-fulfilled-promise made Stewart's next instruction more likely to be followed, which is why she built outsized influence relative to other food personalities.

To illustrate the naming of his own company as a CTA, Hormozi describes naming his holding company Acquisition.com specifically so that the company name was itself a call to action. He recounts a person showing up at his building and asking 'How do I apply to Acquisition.com?' — demonstrating that when the company name is the instruction, the audience follows it without needing an additional explicit CTA.

Hormozi uses the Old Spice ad as the highest-converting example of humor-plus-education in advertising history, noting it took a non-market-leader brand and made it the category share dominator. He attributes this to the ad being both funny (broad reach, lowered resistance) and educational about the product's differentiation (behavior change toward purchase).

Hormozi compares Yelp restaurant selection to illustrate review volume as the dominant trust signal: given a choice between a 5-star restaurant with 3 reviews and a 4.6-star restaurant with 4,000 reviews, he argues any rational consumer chooses the 4,000-review option because volume implies operational track record and consistent service delivery at scale.

practices.text: Never run an ad without a deliberate headline. Every ad has a headline — the choice is only between a bad one (written by default) and a good one (written intentionally).
Test headline and hook ideas by reviewing the first three seconds of organic content and competitor ads — visually and verbally — before writing new headlines from scratch.
Steal hooks across industries: adapt headline formats that are working in travel or weight loss and apply them to your own category.
Write down all product flaws and customer complaints, then claim them proactively in copy using the 'X [flaw] but Y [benefit]' structure before prospects surface them as objections.

For each benefit in your copy, apply the What-Who-When status extension: identify what the benefit is, who (family, colleagues, rivals) awards the resulting status, and in what time period (past, present, future) — generating multiple angles from a single benefit.
Enforce urgency and scarcity limits without exception: say no to buyers who arrive after the deadline or after the quantity limit is reached so that future scarcity is believed.

Always include a PS statement in long-form copy. Use it for: (a) a disclaimer of who the offer is not for, (b) a single-sentence recap of the core persuasion points, or (c) a trained reward for readers who always read the PS (jokes, fun content that occasionally carries the CTA).
In multi-step funnels, tell the prospect exactly what will happen at each next step and then deliver precisely that outcome, repeating promise-fulfillment cycles to compound future compliance.

Run all ad copy through a free reading-level tool and edit until it tests at third-grade reading level. Prefer common longer words over shorter but unfamiliar words (simplicity over concision). Use short sentences, active verbs ('he sprinted' not 'he ran quickly'), and few adverbs.

Describe the experience of the desired outcome rather than the outcome itself: instead of 'get more leads,' describe the moment — 'salespeople can't write down credit card numbers fast enough because customers are reading them too fast.' Show the future problem they would prefer to have.

Document and substantiate every result, transformation, and client you have helped. Volume of substantiated proof (reviews, testimonials, case studies) compounds into implied authority and long-term competitive moat.
